Westpoint

A web ERP plus driver and passenger apps for a charter bus company in Singapore. I ended up its only designer, owning 15+ modules.

RoleSenior Product Designer. Joined in a design team. Became the only designer when my lead resigned.
UsersOperators, drivers and invited passengers
ScopeWeb ERP (15+ modules), driver app, passenger app
Client work under NDA. Research material and before-and-after comparisons stay private. Figures are my own project estimates, not a controlled study.

The main problem

The company was revamping the whole platform: ERP-like and end to end, not one screen or one module. When I joined, design had more than fifteen modules to cover. The hardest logic sat around drivers and contracts.

The data flow was the hidden UX.

The old system grew through thousands of iterations without an in-house tech team. Some modules were complex and never split, so how the data moved was as confusing as the screens.

The users are not tech-heavy.

Operators, drivers and passengers range widely in confidence, and some are older. The brief asked for interfaces that feel general and standard, not clever.

The business could not stop.

New iterations kept arriving while the revamp was under way, so design needed better operations and structure, not just better screens.

How I work

A lighter system and feedback in small steps, so one designer could keep more than fifteen modules moving.

Simplify the system

Design system cut from five levels to three, built from components developers use as they are.

PRD, then master screen

One screen per module validated with product, so development starts in week 1.

Details, then states

Each step checked before the next, so a wrong direction is caught early.

Research for mobile

A research framework the product team adopted, after two years of assumption-led attempts.

Prototype to unblock

A vibe-coded, feature-flagged prototype on the real repo moved live tracking after 4 months.

Regular feedback

Short reviews at every step, so nothing is missed and nothing is redone at the end.

How it flows

One trip, three apps

The same trip as it moves from the operations roster to the driver and the passenger.

  1. 1
    Roster

    Operations see a month of standby, AM, PM and leave, with gaps counted up front.

  2. 2
    Driver starts the day

    Today’s progress and the active trip come first.

  3. 3
    Start trip

    Numbered stops, the first pick-up and passenger count, then one START TRIP.

  4. 4
    On the road

    The next turn in large type, arrival and wait time side by side. SOS always in reach.

  5. 5
    Passenger waits

    ETA, plate and driver on one card; a QR ticket one tap away.

  6. 6
    Live board

    Operations see every trip; trips that need action are counted by reason.

The complex parts

Coverage before anyone opens a day

Why it’s hard

A missing standby driver is found too late if you have to open each day.

How it’s solved
  • Unassigned standby and AM/PM shifts for the next 60 days lead the page.
  • One colour per shift state across the whole month; zero standby turns red.

Trips that need someone now

Why it’s hard

Red alone doesn’t say what to do.

How it’s solved
  • Driver offline, late at first point, about to be late, next trip delayed and SOS each get a count that filters the board.
  • Map and list share one filter, and each card carries its next action.

Read while driving

Why it’s hard

Drivers glance at the screen between turns.

How it’s solved
  • The next turn is the biggest text in the app.
  • Arrival and wait time sit together; leaving the route asks first.

A closed service for invited riders

Why it’s hard

Passengers belong to client companies; strangers must not join.

How it’s solved
  • Riders join with a code from their company administrator.
  • They pick their recurring trips once, so home only shows rides they take.

Looking back

Simple is a decision.

For people working a busy shift, familiar beats fancy. The craft is in mapping the right data to the right screen.

Owning the logic changes the work.

Once there was nobody to hand the hard questions to, flows and data became my design material as much as layouts.

Give people something to try.

A clickable, flagged prototype on the real repo moved a decision that static screens had not moved in four months.
